query: W is attractive for plasma-facing divertor components because of its high melting point, thermal resistance, low sputtering yield, and low tritium retention, but its relatively high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature limits use. CuCrZr provides favorable thermal conductivity as a heat sink but has a narrow operating-temperature range and is susceptible to irradiation embrittlement, requiring an intermediate layer that transfers heat efficiently while keeping both materials within suitable temperature ranges. Earlier HEA studies reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, thermal stability in Mo6.6Nb6Ni80Ta1.4Ti6, and favorable combinations of strength and ductility in NbTaTiV, HfNbTaTiZr, and TiVNbTa. Nevertheless, HEA performance can involve tradeoffs among strength, ductility, thermal stability, and phase constitution. TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC dendritic state combines about 800 MPa yield strength with approximately 40% strain, but its reported yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K are only 330 and 423 MPa, respectively, at 30% strain. Under the constraints of efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer, high-temperature mechanical stability, and compatibility with the limited operating ranges of both adjoining materials, what single intervention could improve the TiVNbTa intermediate material? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted change relative to the reported TiVNbTa baseline, temperature and loading boundaries, supporting evidence from the prior HEA results, and a controlled experiment that would falsify both the performance prediction and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of chromium (Cr) to the TiVNbTa high‐entropy alloy will induce a multiphase microstructure that enhances high-temperature strength and thermal stability while maintaining its room-temperature ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC dendritic state with ~800 MPa yield strength at room temperature and reduced strengths (330 MPa yield, 423 MPa compressive) at 1273 K, along with high ductility (approximately 40% strain at RT and 30% at high temperature).
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled trace addition of Cr (on the order of a few atomic percent, similar in scale to the Cr0.75 addition used in related RHEAs) into the TiVNbTa alloy.
generation.conditions: Component operating in plasma-facing divertor conditions, with the intermediate alloy required to transfer heat efficiently between W and CuCrZr, maintaining performance at temperatures up to about 1273 K under mechanical strains near 30%.
generation.structural_mediator: The Cr addition is expected to promote the formation of a secondary reinforcing phase (such as a Laves phase or a second BCC phase) alongside the primary BCC matrix, leading to a triphasic or multiphase microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Cr atoms drive phase separation during alloy processing, resulting in uniformly distributed secondary phases. These phases redistribute local compressive stresses and impede dislocation motion, which enhances yield and compressive strength at elevated temperatures while not significantly impairing ductility at room temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: An anticipated ~20–30% improvement in high-temperature yield and compressive strengths relative to the baseline, with only minor, if any, reductions in room-temperature ductility.
generation.baseline: Existing TiVNbTa with a single-phase BCC structure exhibiting approximately 330 MPa yield strength at 1273 K and ~800 MPa at room temperature.
generation.boundary: This improvement is predicted under high-temperature mechanical loads typical of plasma-facing divertor operating conditions (up to 1273 K with strains around 30%). Effects outside these operating conditions remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact scale of strength enhancement and the nature and volume fraction of the induced secondary phases depend on precise alloy composition, processing conditions, and kinetic factors, and thus exact values are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of TiVNbTa samples with varying Cr additions (e.g., 0%, 2%, 5% atomic Cr) under identical processing conditions. Subject each sample to mechanical tests at room temperature and at 1273 K with controlled strain rates. In parallel, perform microstructural characterization (using XRD, SEM, and TEM) to identify phase constitution and distribution.
measurements: High-temperature (1273 K) yield strength and compressive strength
Phase identification and volume fraction via XRD and microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Cr-doped TiVNbTa samples fail to exhibit at least a 20–30% improvement in high-temperature mechanical strengths relative to the Cr-free baseline, or if the anticipated secondary reinforcing phase does not form in significant amounts, the hypothesis and the proposed mechanism are falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractOvercoming the strength-ductility trade-off in refractory-based high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) is challenging. In this work, simultaneous strength-ductility enhancement of as-cast HfMoTaTiZrCrx refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) was attained through Cr addition. Experimental results reveal that Cr addition induces a unique triphasic microstructure, comprising a Hf/Ti/Zr-enriched BCC1 phase, a Mo/Ta-dominated BCC2 phase, and a Cr/Mo/Ta-dominated C15-type Laves phase. The optimized HfMoTaTiZrCr0.75 alloy achieves σ0.2 of 1982.7 MPa (28% higher than Cr-free HfMoTaTiZr RHEAs) and εf of 12.4% (65% enhancement), representing an outstanding strength among reported as-cast RHEAs with comparable ductility. Microstructural analysis suggests that the uniformly distributed BCC phase redistributes compressive stress and suppresses crack propagation, while the Laves phase enhances strength through Laves phase-induced dislocation obstruction. Simultaneous strength-ductility enhancement of HfMoTaTiZrCrx RHEAs was attained.
